title: What is lock downgrading in ReentrantReadWriteLock, why is downgrading from write to read safe while upgrading from read to write is not supported, and when is downgrading useful?

s1_definition.profdef: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` allows many concurrent readers or a single exclusive writer. Lock downgrading is the pattern where a thread that holds the write lock acquires the read lock before releasing the write lock, thereby moving from exclusive write access to shared read access without ever releasing all protection. This is explicitly supported and safe. The reverse, upgrading from a held read lock to the write lock, is not supported: if two threads both hold the read lock and both try to upgrade, each waits for the other to release its read lock, producing a deadlock, so the JVM does not allow it. Downgrading is useful when a thread must perform a write and then immediately read the fresh result while guaranteeing no other writer can intervene.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India master interest-rate sheet. The write lock is like locking yourself alone in the records room to change the rate — nobody else can enter. Downgrading is the safe move where, after changing the rate, you prop the door open to reading mode (acquire read lock) and only then step back from the exclusive write lock, so you are still guaranteed to read the exact value you just wrote, with no other editor sneaking in between. Upgrading is the dangerous move: two auditors are both already reading in the room (both hold read locks), and both now want to become the sole editor. Each refuses to leave until the other leaves, so they stand there forever — a deadlock. That is why the lock simply forbids read-to-write upgrade.
s1_definition.oneliner: Downgrade safely by taking the read lock before releasing the write lock; never try to upgrade read to write because two readers both upgrading deadlock, which is why the JVM does not support it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ReentrantReadWriteLock` allows many concurrent readers or a single exclusive writer. Lock downgrading is the pattern where a thread that holds the write lock acquires the read lock before releasing the write lock, thereby moving from exclusive write access to shared read access without ever releasing all protection. This is explicitly supported and safe. The reverse, upgrading from a held read lock to the write lock, is not supported: if two threads both hold the read lock and both try to upgrade, each waits for the other to release its read lock, producing a deadlock, so the JVM does not allow it. Downgrading is useful when a thread must perform a write and then immediately read the fresh result while guaranteeing no other writer can intervene.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India master interest-rate sheet. The write lock is like locking yourself alone in the records room to change the rate — nobody else can enter. Downgrading is the safe move where, after changing the rate, you prop the door open to reading mode (acquire read lock) and only then step back from the exclusive write lock, so you are still guaranteed to read the exact value you just wrote, with no other editor sneaking in between. Upgrading is the dangerous move: two auditors are both already reading in the room (both hold read locks), and both now want to become the sole editor. Each refuses to leave until the other leaves, so they stand there forever — a deadlock. That is why the lock simply forbids read-to-write upgrade.

**One line to remember:** Downgrade safely by taking the read lock before releasing the write lock; never try to upgrade read to write because two readers both upgrading deadlock, which is why the JVM does not support it.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores the daily interest rate that many threads read constantly to compute interest for savings accounts like Rajesh's SAV2001. A few times a day the treasury updates the rate. Reads vastly outnumber writes, so a ReentrantReadWriteLock lets all the reader threads run in parallel and only serialize on the rare write.

Problem 2 — When treasury updates the rate, it must then immediately recompute and cache the derived daily factor using the exact new rate, and it must be certain no other writer slips in between the write and that read. If treasury released the write lock and then re-acquired a read lock separately, another writer could change the rate in the gap, so the cached factor would be based on a stale rate. This is exactly what lock downgrading solves: acquire the read lock before releasing the write lock, so protection is continuous.

Problem 3 — A naive developer tries to make a reader thread "promote" itself to writer when it notices the rate is stale, by calling writeLock while holding readLock. Under load, two such reader threads deadlock. The code demonstrates why upgrade is forbidden and shows the correct release-then-acquire-then-recheck workaround.

The code builds a `RateStore` backed by a ReentrantReadWriteLock with a downgrading `updateAndComputeFactor` method, a safe `readRate`, and a demonstration of the forbidden upgrade versus the correct workaround.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a RateStore starting at 6.50 percent, four reader threads, and one writer thread that sets the rate to 7.25 percent and computes the daily factor.

Step 1: The four reader threads each call `readRate`, which acquires the read lock. Because read locks are shared, all four can hold it simultaneously and read 6.50 in parallel without blocking one another.

Step 2: The writer calls `updateAndComputeFactor(7.25)` and acquires the write lock. The write lock is exclusive, so it waits until no reader holds the lock, then blocks any new reader. At this instant the writer is the sole holder.

Step 3: The writer sets `rate = 7.25` (the write). Still holding the write lock, it calls `readLock().lock()`, which succeeds instantly because it is the only holder. Now the writer holds both the write and read locks.

Step 4: The writer releases the write lock in the finally block. It still holds the read lock, so this is the downgrade: it has moved from exclusive write access to shared read access without ever dropping all protection. Crucially, no other writer could have changed the rate in this transition.

Step 5: The writer reads `rate` (guaranteed to be 7.25, the exact value it wrote) and computes the daily factor 7.25 divided by 36500. It then releases the read lock. Finally, the workaround method demonstrates the safe way to write-after-read: release the read lock, acquire the write lock, and re-check the condition, never attempting an in-place upgrade which would deadlock.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: read rate = 6.50
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: read rate = 6.50
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: read rate = 6.50
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: read rate = 6.50
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: writer computed daily factor = 0.0001986301
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: workaround: rate already fresh, no write needed
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  RateStore (ReentrantReadWriteLock), start rate = 6.50
    │
    ├─ 4 readers: readLock (SHARED) ── all read 6.50 in parallel
    │
    ▼
  writer: updateAndComputeFactor(7.25)
    │ writeLock.lock()  (EXCLUSIVE — waits for readers to drain)
    │ rate = 7.25                                 ← WRITE
    │ readLock.lock()   (acquire while holding write) ╗
    │ writeLock.unlock()                              ║ DOWNGRADE
    │ ← now holds only READ lock ─────────────────────╝
    │ read rate = 7.25  (guaranteed fresh, no writer could intervene)
    │ factor = 7.25 / 36500 = 0.0001986301
    │ readLock.unlock()
    ▼
  FORBIDDEN:  readLock held → writeLock.lock() blocks forever (deadlock)
  WORKAROUND: readLock.unlock() → writeLock.lock() → RE-CHECK → write
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ReentrantReadWriteLock Downgrade ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Read-Write Lock: many readers OR one writer             │
  │  Downgrade: write→read without releasing all protection  │
  │     WHY: read the exact value just written, no race gap  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: RateStore only stores/guards rate                    │
  │  O: new derived value = new read-side method             │
  │  D: callers depend on RateStore API, not lock internals  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   ReentrantReadWriteLock (JDK, AQS)   │
  │  + readLock(): Lock   (shared)        │
  │  + writeLock(): Lock  (exclusive)     │
  │  reentrant; write can take read       │
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
          guards   │
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          RateStore                    │
  │  - rate: BigDecimal                   │
  │  - rw: ReentrantReadWriteLock         │ ◆ composition
  │  + readRate(): BigDecimal             │  readLock
  │  + updateAndComputeFactor(r): BigDec  │  DOWNGRADE
  │  + demonstrateCorrectUpgradeWorkaround│  release→write→recheck
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  DOWNGRADE sequence:
    1. writeLock.lock()      (exclusive)
    2. mutate state          (WRITE)
    3. readLock.lock()       (acquire while still write-locked)
    4. writeLock.unlock()    (now holds only read → downgraded)
    5. read fresh state      (READ, no writer can intervene)
    6. readLock.unlock()

  UPGRADE (read→write): NOT SUPPORTED → two upgraders deadlock
  Workaround: unlock read → lock write → RE-CHECK condition → write
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A ReentrantReadWriteLock gives me two locks that share one piece of state: a read lock that many threads can hold at the same time, and a write lock that only one thread can hold and that excludes all readers. It is the right tool when reads vastly outnumber writes, because all the readers run in parallel and only the rare write serializes everyone.

Lock downgrading is the supported and safe pattern where a thread that holds the write lock acquires the read lock before it releases the write lock. The sequence is: take the write lock, mutate the state, then while still holding the write lock take the read lock, and only then release the write lock. After that you still hold the read lock, so you have moved from exclusive write access down to shared read access without ever letting go of all protection. Why this matters is the race window. If instead I released the write lock and then separately re-acquired a read lock, another writer could change the value in that tiny gap, and the value I read would not be the one I just wrote. Downgrading closes that gap entirely, which is why it is perfect when I need to write a value and then immediately read the fresh derived result.

The reverse, upgrading from read to write, is not supported, and for a good reason. If a thread holds the read lock and tries to acquire the write lock, the write lock needs exclusivity but the thread is still holding its own read lock, so it blocks on itself. If two threads both hold the read lock and both try to upgrade, each is waiting for the other to drop its read lock, and neither will, so they deadlock. The lock simply does not allow it. The correct workaround when I discover I need to write after reading is to release the read lock, acquire the write lock, and then re-check the condition, because the state may have changed in the gap.

At National Bank of India I used this on the daily interest rate store. Hundreds of threads read the rate constantly to compute interest for accounts like Rajesh's savings account, and the treasury updated the rate only a few times a day. When treasury updated the rate, it used downgrading to compute and cache the derived daily factor from the exact new value, guaranteeing no other writer slipped in between. And when a developer tried to make a reader promote itself to a writer in place, we caught the deadlock in load testing and replaced it with the release-then-acquire-then-recheck pattern. The sentence I give interviewers is that you downgrade by taking the read lock before releasing the write lock, and you never upgrade read to write because two readers both upgrading will deadlock, which is exactly why the JVM forbids it.

---

keyPoints: Write to read lock: safe, allowed
Read to write lock: NOT allowed, causes deadlock
Pattern: acquire write, modify, acquire read, release write
